loop.label: The closed loop
loop.lead: Many pet brands outsource both the science and the factory. We keep both inside the loop, so what the lab and the production line learn goes straight into the next formula.
loop.s1_p: Our AI-powered research system searches and cross-checks the peer-reviewed literature, so a review that takes a traditional team months takes us days. Our team reviews every ingredient, dose and claim, and every citation traces back to the original paper.
loop.s2_p: Our in-house research facility analyses raw materials and finished products for identity, potency and contaminants, and runs stability tests across shelf life, such as live-culture counts and fish-oil freshness.
loop.s3_p: GMP-certified production in our own facility, with runs as small as 3,000 units, so a product for a single species is possible at all. The same facility supplies fish oil and calming ingredients for one of the world's top-10 pet food brands in Asia.
loop.s4_p: Lab results and production data go back into the research system, so the next formula starts from a better place.

p.calmcat.blurb: A lickable purée stick with alpha-casozepine and L-theanine for cats facing change: new homes, new companions, visitors, travel. Made for cats who refuse chews and capsules.
p.calmcat.evidence.0: In 24 fearful cats fed a calming diet with alpha-casozepine and L-tryptophan or a control diet for 4 weeks, the groups differed on behaviour measures in an unfamiliar room, but not on fear of an unfamiliar person. Cats; a complete diet, not our purée.
p.calmcat.evidence.1: In an open-label study of 33 cats with stress-related signs, L-theanine for 30 days cut the median global stress score from 18 to 5, and 30 of 33 cats improved. No placebo group; cats, given as a tablet.
p.calmcat.evidence.2: A randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 60 cats at the vet gave alpha-casozepine for only 3 to 6 days. The only significant effect was fewer sweaty paws at the high dose. That is why CalmCat is a daily product, not a same-day fix.
p.calmcat.evidence.3: In rats given oral doses from 5 to 50 mg/kg, 15 mg/kg was the lowest effective dose of the casein hydrolysate, with effects similar to diazepam in standard behaviour tests but without its disinhibition. Rats; ingredient only.
p.calmcat.inside.0.name: Alpha-casozepine (milk protein hydrolysate)
p.calmcat.inside.0.role: Calming peptide from milk protein; the calming ingredient with the most published cat research.
p.calmcat.inside.1.name: L-theanine
p.calmcat.inside.1.role: Amino acid from tea leaves; a second calming ingredient, supported by an open-label cat study.
p.calmcat.inside.2.name: Taurine
p.calmcat.inside.2.role: Essential for cats; topped up because heat sterilisation raises the amount cats need.
p.calmcat.inside.3.name: Vitamin B6
p.calmcat.inside.3.role: Cofactor the body uses to make serotonin.
p.calmcat.inside.4.name: Liver digest and savoury amino acids
p.calmcat.inside.4.role: Flavour built on what cats can taste, with no sugar.
p.calmcat.inside.5.name: Tuna and chicken purée
p.calmcat.inside.5.role: The carrier: a lickable treat format cats already finish.
p.calmcat.limits.0: Cat evidence for alpha-casozepine is mixed: a diet study was positive on some measures and a short-course vet-visit trial found little. CalmCat itself has not been tested in cats.
p.calmcat.limits.1: The L-theanine cat data come from one open-label study without a placebo group, and no study has tested the two ingredients together.
p.calmcat.limits.2: Effects build over two to four weeks of daily use. CalmCat is not a same-day product, and it does not replace veterinary care.
p.calmcat.problem: Stress in indoor and multi-cat homes rarely looks dramatic. It looks like a cat that hides when visitors arrive, tension between housemates, or a cat that vanishes the moment the carrier comes out. Many owners have already tried a plug-in diffuser and then a calming chew. The chew is usually where it fails: the best-known calming chew for cats averages around three stars, and in one review only one of four cats would eat it. Capsules mean pilling an already stressed cat. A product the cat refuses delivers nothing.
p.calmcat.research.0: Owner-problem phase first: four market research runs read retailer reviews, owner forums and competitor labels across the US, UK and EU. The pattern was consistent: calming products for cats fail on refusal before efficacy is ever tested.
p.calmcat.research.1: Literature pass: our AI-powered research system ran 103 searches and cross-checked 42 PubMed-indexed papers; our team reviewed every ingredient and claim. Alpha-casozepine had the most controlled cat research of any calming ingredient. We found no cat trials for valerian, magnolia, GABA, ashwagandha or chamomile.
p.calmcat.research.2: A second, stricter pass required a published source for every dose. It removed N-acetyl glucosamine after a six-month placebo-controlled trial in 40 cats found no difference from placebo, and excluded alpha-lipoic acid, about ten times more toxic to cats than reported in dogs.
p.calmcat.research.3: A second, independent research run re-checked every citation. We could not obtain the full text of the earliest positive cat trial, so we do not quote its figures. No study has tested our two calming ingredients together, so we make no synergy claim.
p.calmcat.research.4: Also rejected: CBD (the one clean cat trial found no effect, and it is not permitted in EU feed), melatonin (regulatory status), and sugars, which cats cannot taste and which degrade the actives during heat sterilisation.
p.calmcat.tagline: Daily calming support in a purée cats actually finish
p.calmcat.use: Once a day as a lickable treat, straight from the stick or squeezed onto a spoon. Larger cats may need more; follow the pack. Allow two to four weeks.
p.calmcat.why: We built CalmCat around the one thing every failed product had in common: refusal. The format is a lickable purée stick, the treat format cats already finish, flavoured with liver and the savoury notes cats can taste, with no sugar because cats cannot taste sweet. Inside is alpha-casozepine, the calming ingredient with the most cat research behind it, with L-theanine. We say plainly what the evidence shows, including the trials that found little, and we ask owners to allow two to four weeks.
p.gutdaily.blurb: A one-a-day baked hay biscuit carrying live yeast culture, added after baking, plus a yeast-derived prebiotic. Live count guaranteed to the expiry date, not just at manufacture.
p.gutdaily.evidence.0: In 32 weaned rabbits over 56 days, the group fed Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast plus MOS had the best growth and feed conversion of four diets, with improved digestibility including fibre. Production rabbits; not our biscuit.
p.gutdaily.evidence.1: In 120 weaned rabbits of two breeds, diets with MOS gave higher final body weight and feed intake than the control diet, plus better carcass traits. Production rabbits; MOS as a feed ingredient, not our biscuit.
p.gutdaily.evidence.2: The only pet-rabbit study of our yeast strain was a double-blind crossover in 6 healthy rabbits. The yeast changed none of the measured gut bacteria, body weight or dropping size and weight. Small, but we disclose it.
p.gutdaily.inside.0.name: Live yeast culture (Saccharomyces cerevisiae CNCM I-4407)
p.gutdaily.inside.0.role: The only live culture authorised for rabbits in the EU; applied after baking so it stays alive.
p.gutdaily.inside.1.name: Mannan-oligosaccharides (yeast cell wall)
p.gutdaily.inside.1.role: Prebiotic partner to the yeast; together they outperformed either alone in growing rabbits.
p.gutdaily.inside.2.name: Timothy or meadow hay flour
p.gutdaily.inside.2.role: High-fibre base, specified so the biscuit does not dilute a hay diet.
p.gutdaily.inside.3.name: Guar gum
p.gutdaily.inside.3.role: Binds the biscuit without starch or sugar.
p.gutdaily.inside.4.name: Refined vegetable oil
p.gutdaily.inside.4.role: Coating, held to an oxidation spec, that carries the live culture onto the baked biscuit.
p.gutdaily.inside.5.name: Vanilla
p.gutdaily.inside.5.role: Flavour cue; the only palatant we found with published rabbit data.
p.gutdaily.limits.0: Most evidence for this strain comes from young production rabbits; the only pet-rabbit study was small and found no effect. GutDaily has not yet been tested in animals.
p.gutdaily.limits.1: No study shows that a probiotic prevents digestive emergencies in pet rabbits. A rabbit that stops eating or passing droppings needs a vet within hours.
p.gutdaily.limits.2: The strain is authorised for rabbits in the EU. There is no species-specific evidence for it in guinea pigs or chinchillas.
p.gutdaily.problem: Owners who have been through a digestive slowdown with a rabbit or guinea pig do not forget it: the syringe feeding, the paste in the fridge, the daily photos of droppings, and emergency bills that run into thousands. Many want daily live-culture support around diet changes, moves and stress, but the options fail them. Powders are too dry to stick to food and get left in the bowl. Rescue pastes are made for emergencies and cost over £130 a month if used daily. And the best-loved digestive snacks contain no live culture at all.
p.gutdaily.research.0: Owner-problem phase first: 112 searches across retailers, owner forums and competitor labels. Owners who had lived through a digestive emergency wanted daily support, but powders would not stick to food and the best-loved digestive snacks contained no live organism.
p.gutdaily.research.1: Literature pass: our AI-powered research system extracted eleven controlled rabbit trials into one dose table; our team checked the arithmetic. We chose the strain from the EU feed-additive register, so the product is legal for rabbits from day one rather than retrofitted.
p.gutdaily.research.2: A second, stricter pass changed the concept. One small biscuit is a minor share of daily intake, so it cannot be a fibre supplement; hay does that job. Baking destroys cultures, so the live yeast goes on after baking.
p.gutdaily.research.3: Rejected: a Lactobacillus 'restores the flora' story (Lactobacillus is not a dominant rabbit gut genus and dies in baking), an Enterococcus strain without EU rabbit authorisation, and, for now, sodium butyrate, after a liver enzyme rose in a 600-rabbit trial.
p.gutdaily.tagline: A live-culture hay biscuit they eat as a treat
p.gutdaily.use: Give as a daily treat; follow the pack for your species, as chinchillas get less. Keep the pouch sealed, cool and dry to protect the live culture.
p.gutdaily.why: GutDaily delivers a live culture in the one format small herbivores take willingly: a treat. We chose Saccharomyces cerevisiae CNCM I-4407, the only live culture authorised for rabbits in the EU, and apply it after baking, because baking destroys about 99% of live cultures. A yeast-derived prebiotic comes with it. The biscuit itself is grass hay, bound without starch or sugar, and specified so it does not dilute a hay diet. The live count is guaranteed to the expiry date.
p.omega-cat.blurb: Marine EPA and DHA in a single-serve, nitrogen-flushed tuna purée. The omega-3 content is printed on the carton, and each batch comes with a freshness certificate.
p.omega-cat.evidence.0: In a crossover trial in 10 healthy adult cats (and 12 dogs), 84 days of a PUFA-rich oil blend improved coat flexibility, brightness and skin condition scores; hair breaking force rose 5.79% in cats, and serum triglycerides rose 13.16%. An oil blend, not our sachet.
p.omega-cat.evidence.1: In 24 cats fed fish-oil or algal-oil foods at matched DHA levels over three 5-week periods, serum DHA rose similarly, but serum EPA was higher with fish oil. Cats; complete foods, not our sachet.
p.omega-cat.evidence.2: In 72 people given about 3.3 g of EPA plus DHA daily for 2 weeks, re-esterified triglyceride oil showed 124% bioavailability relative to natural fish oil, ethyl esters 73%. Studied in humans, not cats.
p.omega-cat.evidence.3: In 8 healthy cats given purified EPA and DHA daily for 2 months, plasma EPA and DHA rose significantly with no change in bleeding time or platelet aggregation. Cats; purified fatty acids, not our sachet.
p.omega-cat.inside.0.name: Marine fish oil concentrate (re-esterified triglyceride)
p.omega-cat.inside.0.role: Source of EPA and DHA, in the concentrate form with the highest measured absorption.
p.omega-cat.inside.1.name: Tuna
p.omega-cat.inside.1.role: Carrier and flavour: a purée cats lick willingly, held to a strict mercury specification.
p.omega-cat.inside.2.name: Vitamin E
p.omega-cat.inside.2.role: Dosed to the feline guideline for added fish oil, protecting the omega-3 inside the body.
p.omega-cat.inside.3.name: Mixed tocopherols, rosemary extract and ascorbyl palmitate
p.omega-cat.inside.3.role: Antioxidants in the oil that slow rancidity in the sachet.
p.omega-cat.inside.4.name: Trisodium citrate
p.omega-cat.inside.4.role: Binds the iron from tuna that would otherwise speed oxidation of the oil.
p.omega-cat.limits.0: Our dose is matched to published cat trials, but those trials used complete diets or oil blends. Omega Cat itself has not been tested in cats yet.
p.omega-cat.limits.1: Visible coat changes take 8 to 12 weeks. We sell Omega Cat for skin and coat only; other claims would need a higher intake or a complete diet.
p.omega-cat.limits.2: Heat sterilisation could reduce omega-3 or raise oxidation in the sachet. Our lab is measuring both in the finished product before launch.
p.omega-cat.problem: Owners buy fish oil for their cat's skin and coat, then find the cat will not touch food with oil on it. Pump bottles leak and make a mess, and once opened the oil oxidises: owners describe brown residue floating in oil they suspect has gone bad. Lickable alternatives solve the taste problem, but the leading one declares no EPA or DHA at all, so owners cannot tell what their cat is getting. And when we checked, no pet fish-oil brand published oxidation values or a batch certificate of analysis.
p.omega-cat.research.0: Owner-problem phase: retailer reviews, owner forums and competitor label panels. The top complaints were refusal, leaking pumps and rancid oil. We checked every pet fish-oil brand we could find for published oxidation data or batch certificates and found none.
p.omega-cat.research.1: Literature pass: our AI-powered research system ran 60 searches and drew on 51 PubMed-indexed papers; our team reviewed every claim. Finding: cats have no established safe upper limit for EPA and DHA. The often-quoted figure is a dog value, so we set our own.
p.omega-cat.research.2: A second, independent research run proposed a lower, DHA-led dose. We compared both against the published cat trials, kept the dose that matches their exposure, and added a smaller serving for small cats to protect the safety margin.
p.omega-cat.research.3: Rejected: plant omega-3 such as flax or chia (cats convert it poorly to DHA), DHA-only algal oil (less EPA), ethyl-ester concentrates (lower absorption), and free vitamin C, which can speed oxidation alongside the iron in tuna.
p.omega-cat.tagline: Omega-3 for skin and coat, in a purée cats finish
p.omega-cat.use: Once a day from the sachet or over food; use straight after opening. Small cats need less. Ask your vet first if your cat takes anticoagulants, NSAIDs or aspirin.
p.omega-cat.why: Omega Cat puts a declared amount of marine EPA and DHA into a tuna purée cats lick willingly, sealed in a nitrogen-flushed single-serve sachet, so there is no open bottle to go rancid. The oil is a re-esterified triglyceride concentrate, the form with the highest absorption among the concentrates compared in a controlled study. We matched the dose to the daily EPA and DHA intake in the positive controlled cat trials, added vitamin E to protect the oil in the body, and link a freshness certificate to every batch.
p.plumacalm.blurb: A stick-pack powder for parrots built on insoluble fibre, the best-studied diet factor in feather pecking, plus L-tryptophan, alpha-casozepine and L-theanine. Sprinkled on damp food.
p.plumacalm.evidence.0: In laying hens fed diets with 3%, 6% or 9% insoluble fibre, severe feather pecking fell from 0.78 to 0.31 to 0.12 pecks per 30 minutes per hen (P<0.0001), plumage stayed better and laying performance was unchanged. Hens, not parrots.
p.plumacalm.evidence.1: In 1,600 laying hens fed from 16 to 50 weeks of age, a diet higher in insoluble fibre improved feather cover (P=0.016) and reduced rear-body pecking injuries (P=0.012). Hens, not parrots.
p.plumacalm.evidence.2: In growing bantams, adding L-tryptophan to the diet at 20 g/kg suppressed feather-pecking damage compared with no added tryptophan. Bantams, not parrots, and at a higher dietary level than our stick provides.
p.plumacalm.evidence.3: In 160 laying hens, acute tryptophan depletion induced gentle, repetitive feather pecking in all three genetic lines tested, linking the serotonin system to pecking. Hens; a mechanism study, not a supplement trial.
p.plumacalm.inside.0.name: Insoluble fibre (lignocellulose)
p.plumacalm.inside.0.role: The lead active: more insoluble fibre cut severe feather pecking in controlled hen trials.
p.plumacalm.inside.1.name: L-tryptophan
p.plumacalm.inside.1.role: Serotonin precursor; in hens, low tryptophan is linked to more feather pecking.
p.plumacalm.inside.2.name: Alpha-casozepine (milk protein hydrolysate)
p.plumacalm.inside.2.role: Calming peptide shared with our cat and rabbit lines; its receptor target is conserved in birds.
p.plumacalm.inside.3.name: L-theanine
p.plumacalm.inside.3.role: Amino acid from tea leaves; a gentle second calming ingredient with a wide safety margin.
p.plumacalm.inside.4.name: DL-methionine and biotin
p.plumacalm.inside.4.role: Sulphur amino acid and vitamin the bird uses to build feather keratin.
p.plumacalm.inside.5.name: Millet, banana and anise
p.plumacalm.inside.5.role: Familiar tastes and smells so wary birds accept the powder on their food.
p.plumacalm.limits.0: No study has tested alpha-casozepine in any bird, and the fibre and tryptophan evidence comes from chickens, not parrots.
p.plumacalm.limits.1: PlumaCalm has not yet been tested in parrots. Our research calls for acceptance and small-bird tolerance studies before launch.
p.plumacalm.limits.2: Feather plucking often has medical causes, so see an avian vet first. Allow four to eight weeks; new feathers depend on the moult.
p.plumacalm.pack: 30 sticks × 1 g (size L) or × 0.3 g (size S)
p.plumacalm.problem: Owners of greys, cockatoos, cockatiels and conures dealing with feather plucking, screaming or night frights have usually done the vet workup, added UV lighting and foraging toys, and paid month after month for supplements that did nothing. Dosing is its own battle: forcing powder into the beak of a bird that hates it, or adding it to drinking water, where small birds often fail to take in a reliable dose. The one calming product built on a studied mechanism has a single active, costs a lot and is often out of stock.
p.plumacalm.research.0: Owner-problem phase: retailer listings, reviews and owner forums. Owners had tried everything; dosing failed in the beak or the water bowl; and one of Europe's largest pet retailers listed no bird calming product at all.
p.plumacalm.research.1: Literature pass: our AI-powered research system cross-checked 71 PubMed-indexed papers; our team reviewed each claim. Pigeon GABA-A receptor subunits are 94.6-96.3% identical to reference sequences, so the peptide's target exists in birds, but no study has measured its absorption in any bird.
p.plumacalm.research.2: A second, stricter pass found the laying-hen fibre trials and changed the formula: the carrier became the lead active, and a maltodextrin carrier was ruled out for good.
p.plumacalm.research.3: Safety shaped the format. Small budgerigars have a thin margin against rodent safety data, so small birds get a separate, smaller stick. No added iron, calcium, vitamin D3, vitamin A or sodium; every anise lot is identity-tested to exclude star anise.
p.plumacalm.species: Parrots, cockatoos, cockatiels, conures and budgerigars
p.plumacalm.tagline: Daily calm and feather support, sprinkled on fresh food
p.plumacalm.use: Sprinkle one stick over damp chopped vegetables or soaked pellets, mix, and serve within 15 minutes. Not on dry seed or in water. Choose the stick size by bird weight.
p.plumacalm.why: We started from the evidence, not the trend. The best-studied dietary lever for feather pecking in birds is insoluble fibre, so in PlumaCalm the carrier is the lead active, not filler. To it we add L-tryptophan, the serotonin precursor linked to pecking in hens, the same calming peptide as our cat and small-mammal lines, and L-theanine. It is pre-dosed in two sizes by bird weight, with millet, banana and anise cues for wary birds, and no added iron.
p.reptile-probiotics.blurb: Five live microorganisms plus vitamin B1 in a powder dosed by your reptile's body weight, with an honest account of what reptile research does and does not show.
p.reptile-probiotics.evidence.0: In a 52-week trial in 30 musk turtles, a multi-strain probiotic including L. acidophilus, B. bifidum and E. faecium raised weight gain to 7.22 g versus 5.63 g in controls (P=0.045) and increased shell calcium and phosphorus. Turtles; a different blend.
p.reptile-probiotics.evidence.1: In 216 juvenile Reeves' turtles fed for up to 120 days, Bacillus subtilis improved weight gain rate and survival and increased intestinal villus height and width versus a control diet. Turtles; a single-strain feed additive, not our blend.
p.reptile-probiotics.evidence.2: In 24 juvenile soft-shelled turtles over 6 weeks, Enterococcus faecium did not change growth, but goblet cells rose 1.5-fold, villus measures and intestinal IgA increased, and Aeromonas fell. Turtles; a single strain, not our blend.
p.reptile-probiotics.evidence.3: Seven alligators fed only gizzard shad, a thiaminase-rich fish, fell to 25-50% of their starting blood and muscle thiamine over 6-12 months; three died, and two given thiamine recovered normal levels. Alligators; vitamin B1, not probiotics.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.0.name: Bacillus subtilis
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.0.role: Spore-forming culture that keeps well in storage; improved weight gain and survival in a 216-turtle trial.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.1.name: Lactobacillus acidophilus and Lactobacillus casei
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.1.role: Lactic acid bacteria; L. acidophilus was part of the blend that raised musk turtle growth.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.2.name: Enterococcus faecium
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.2.role: Improved gut-lining structure and immune markers in soft-shelled turtles, though growth did not change.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.3.name: Bifidobacterium bifidum
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.3.role: Part of the multi-strain blend linked to better growth and shell minerals in musk turtles.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.4.name: Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.4.role: For fish-fed reptiles: some fish contain thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys vitamin B1.
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.5.name: Amylase and zinc
p.reptile-probiotics.inside.5.role: A starch-digesting enzyme and a trace mineral; no reptile study tests either, so we claim nothing for them.
p.reptile-probiotics.limits.0: Every controlled reptile probiotic trial we found was in aquatic or semi-aquatic turtles. Use in lizards, snakes, geckos and land tortoises is extrapolation.
p.reptile-probiotics.limits.1: Results are mixed, and Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium are not core reptile gut bacteria, so expect passing support rather than permanent colonisation.
p.reptile-probiotics.limits.2: This product has not itself been tested in reptiles. It is not a treatment for parasites or infection; follow your vet's advice.
p.reptile-probiotics.problem: Keepers reach for a probiotic after a deworming or veterinary treatment course, after brumation or hibernation, or when a new animal arrives. The products on the shelf give them little to go on. Most tell a 20 g gecko and a 15 kg sulcata tortoise to take the same serving. Some are dosed through drinking water, which reptiles drink little of and which, warm in a vivarium, grows bacteria of its own. Because nothing on the label tells them what they are getting, some keepers give human probiotics off-label instead.
p.reptile-probiotics.research.0: This product was already selling, so we asked a different question: what evidence exists for the category, and does our dosing make sense? Most of 119 searches went to keeper forums, label panels and patents, because the science is thin.
p.reptile-probiotics.research.1: Our AI-powered research system searched and cross-checked the literature, and our team reviewed every finding. Seven in-vivo records exist in total: six in farmed aquatic or semi-aquatic turtles, one an uncontrolled iguana report. No controlled trial exists in any lizard, snake, gecko or land tortoise.
p.reptile-probiotics.research.2: We kept the null and negative results in view: growth did not change in yellow-bellied sliders or soft-shelled turtles, and one Bacillus subtilis strain given alone reduced gut villus height in musk turtles.
p.reptile-probiotics.research.3: A label-by-label review of six competing reptile probiotics found only one dosing by body weight, and one delivering everything through drinking water. Every reptile trial gave probiotics in food, so that is how we tell keepers to use ours.
p.reptile-probiotics.tagline: Multi-strain live cultures for reptiles, dosed by body weight
p.reptile-probiotics.use: Dust feeder insects, sprinkle on lightly misted greens, or roll thawed prey in it while damp. Dose by body weight per the pack. Never add to drinking or soaking water.
p.reptile-probiotics.why: Our research found that the one long-term positive reptile probiotic trial used a multi-strain blend sharing three of our organisms, so we keep the blend multi-strain. It is dosed by body weight, because a gecko and a giant tortoise do not need the same amount. It carries vitamin B1 for fish-fed reptiles, since some fish contain an enzyme that destroys it. And we say plainly where the evidence stops: almost all of it comes from turtles.
p.settle.blurb: A hay-flour topper with alpha-casozepine and L-tryptophan for rabbits, guinea pigs and chinchillas facing change. Herb-free, because common calming herbs relax gut muscle.
p.settle.evidence.0: In rats given oral doses from 5 to 50 mg/kg, 15 mg/kg was the lowest effective dose of the casein hydrolysate, with effects in standard behaviour tests similar to diazepam but without the disinhibition diazepam caused. Rats; ingredient only.
p.settle.evidence.1: In rats, the hydrolysate at 15 mg/kg had calming effects like diazepam and still worked after 7 days of twice-daily dosing when diazepam did not; memory retention was better than with diazepam and no place preference developed. Rats; ingredient only.
p.settle.evidence.2: In mice given 75 to 500 mg/kg by mouth, the hydrolysate did not significantly change locomotor activity or motor function in open-field and rota-rod tests. Mice; ingredient only.
p.settle.evidence.3: Why Settle is herb-free: in isolated rabbit jejunum, chamomile extract at 0.003 to 0.013 mg/mL reduced spontaneous gut muscle contractions in a concentration-dependent way, similar to the drug verapamil. Rabbit tissue in the lab, not live rabbits.
p.settle.inside.0.name: Alpha-casozepine (milk protein hydrolysate)
p.settle.inside.0.role: Milk-derived calming peptide; in rodents it calmed without impairing movement, which matters for a prey animal.
p.settle.inside.1.name: L-tryptophan
p.settle.inside.1.role: Amino acid the body uses to make serotonin, which also supports normal gut movement in rabbits.
p.settle.inside.2.name: Timothy or meadow hay flour
p.settle.inside.2.role: Familiar, high-fibre carrier the animal already eats, ground coarse enough to resist sorting.
p.settle.inside.3.name: Lucerne meal and apple pomace
p.settle.inside.3.role: Natural flavour so the granules taste like food, not medicine.
p.settle.inside.4.name: Acacia gum
p.settle.inside.4.role: Light coating that helps granules cling to damp greens so they are not picked out.
p.settle.limits.0: No study has tested alpha-casozepine in rabbits, guinea pigs or chinchillas, and controlled trials in cats at the vet and in foals found little or no effect. Settle's case is extrapolated from rodents.
p.settle.limits.1: Settle has not yet been tested in animals. Our research calls for gut-tolerance and acceptance studies before launch.
p.settle.limits.2: It is a calming support, not a treatment. A rabbit that has not eaten for 12 hours needs a vet.
p.settle.problem: For rabbit and guinea pig owners, stress is not just a behaviour problem. Bonding a second rabbit, moving house, recovering from neutering or travelling can put a small herbivore off its food, and owners know a rabbit that stops eating needs a vet fast. A failed bonding can end in an emergency vet visit. What is on offer is mostly herb biscuits with no dose on the pack, some containing comfrey or kava. Loose herbs get refused: one owner sprinkled chamomile on the hay and her rabbit refused the whole pile.
p.settle.research.0: Owner-problem phase: rabbit owner forums, retailer listings and reviews in the US, UK and EU. Owners feared a stressed animal going off its food more than the stress itself. Two of three category leaders contained comfrey and one contained kava, both linked to liver harm.
p.settle.research.1: Literature pass: our AI-powered research system ran 65 searches and cross-checked 54 PubMed-indexed papers; our team reviewed each one. No study of alpha-casozepine exists in any rabbit, guinea pig or chinchilla, so the dose is scaled by body weight from rat studies.
p.settle.research.2: A second, stricter pass removed every herb. Chamomile and a valerian species relaxed isolated rabbit gut tissue, and lemon balm depressed gut contractions in sheep tissue. Slowing the hindgut is exactly what a rabbit should avoid.
p.settle.research.3: A second, independent research run flagged that digesting milk protein can release opioid-like peptides that slow gut transit in lab models. It is a class risk, not shown at our dose, so our research calls for a gut-tolerance study before launch.
p.settle.tagline: Herb-free calm for bonding, new homes and travel
p.settle.use: Sprinkle on damp greens once a day, fed separately. Start at least five days before a planned change and continue throughout. Smaller species may need less; see the pack.
p.settle.why: We wanted a calming product that respects how a rabbit's gut works. Settle uses alpha-casozepine, the same milk-derived calming peptide as our cat and bird lines, with L-tryptophan, on a carrier of hay flour the animal already recognises. Each sachet is pre-dosed, so owners know what every animal gets, and it is herb-free by design. We are open that this is an extrapolation: the dose is scaled from rodent studies, and no one has yet tested it in rabbits.
